Technical Guide

Machining PTFE: Design & Tolerance Guide

PTFE is easy to cut but hard to hold to size. Understanding why helps you design parts that can be made — and inspected — to your drawing.

Because PTFE cannot be injection moulded, most precision PTFE parts — bushes, seals, valve seats, spacers and insulators — are machined from moulded or extruded rod, tube and sheet. PTFE cuts easily, but it is soft, it expands a lot with temperature and it can move after machining. Designing with those facts in mind avoids drawings that look reasonable on paper but are difficult to make or to measure.

How PTFE behaves on the machine

Soft, low-modulus material

Virgin PTFE is soft (about 50–60 Shore D) and has a low modulus, so it deflects under cutting forces instead of shearing cleanly. Blunt tools push and smear the material rather than cutting it, leaving poor finishes and oversize or undersize features.

  • Sharp tools are essential. Ground, polished cutting edges with a positive rake and generous clearance give a clean shear.
  • Light finishing passes reduce deflection and the pressure on the part.
  • Filled grades are abrasive. Glass, carbon and bronze fillers wear tool edges much faster than virgin PTFE, so harder tool materials are generally used for them.

Heat

PTFE conducts heat poorly, so heat generated at the cut stays in the workpiece near the surface. Because PTFE expands far more than metals — roughly ten times as much as steel — a part that is warm when measured on the machine will shrink as it cools. Keep cutting heat low with sharp tools and suitable speeds and feeds, and allow parts to return to room temperature before final measurement.

Never let the material overheat. PTFE releases hazardous fumes if heated well beyond its service temperature, so swarf and dust should be collected and kept away from smoking materials and naked flames.

Coolant

PTFE does not absorb water, and coolant is mainly used to control heat and help clear chips rather than to lubricate. Water-based coolants or compressed air are common. For parts going into food, pharmaceutical or high-purity service, agree on any coolant use and the cleaning required before machining.

Chips and burrs

Virgin PTFE tends to form long, continuous chips that wrap around tools and work, and soft, flexible burrs on edges and cross-holes. Chip control and sharp tools reduce burring; remaining burrs are usually trimmed by hand with a sharp blade. Abrasive deburring methods can embed particles in the soft surface, which matters for sealing faces and purity-critical parts.

Clamping distortion

Because PTFE is soft, heavy chuck or vice pressure deforms the part. It is then machined “true” while distorted and springs back out of shape when released — a classic cause of oval bores and out-of-flat faces. Light clamping pressure, soft or full-contact jaws, spreading the load over a large area and, for thin sheet parts, vacuum fixturing all help.

Dimensional stability

Thermal expansion

PTFE’s high thermal expansion means a part’s size depends noticeably on its temperature. This affects measurement in the workshop, but also service: a bush that fits correctly at 25 °C may bind or loosen at 150 °C. Calculate fits and clearances across the full operating temperature range, not just at assembly.

The ~19 °C transition

PTFE goes through a crystalline transition at about 19 °C, with a further smaller one near 30 °C, producing a step change in volume of the order of 1 %. Because this sits right at typical workshop temperature, small swings in room temperature produce disproportionately large changes in measured size. For close-tolerance parts:

  • state on the drawing the temperature at which dimensions apply, for example 23 °C ± 2 °C;
  • condition parts at that temperature for long enough to stabilise through their thickness before measuring;
  • agree the measurement temperature between supplier and customer, so both inspections compare like with like.

Residual stress and stress relief

Moulded PTFE stock can contain residual stresses from moulding and sintering. Machining away material releases some of that stress, and the part can continue to move for some time afterwards — bores close up, rings go oval, flat parts bow. For precision parts, stock can be stress-relieved (annealed) before machining, or parts can be rough-machined, annealed and then finish-machined. Annealing means heating to a controlled temperature below the melting point, holding, then cooling slowly. If stress relief matters for your part, state it on the drawing.

Designing for tolerance

PTFE cannot be held to the same tolerances as metal parts in the same size range, and the measured result depends on temperature. The most useful step a designer can take is to separate functional dimensions from everything else:

  • identify the few features that genuinely control function — a sealing diameter, a running clearance, a seat face — and tolerance those carefully;
  • apply general tolerances to the rest, so effort and inspection go where they matter;
  • allow for the part’s behaviour in service: creep under load, expansion with temperature and, in filled grades, slightly better stability than virgin.
FeatureWhy it is a problem in PTFEDesign guidance
Tight tolerances everywhereExpansion, the ~19 °C transition and stress relaxation all move dimensionsApply tight tolerances only to functional features; use general tolerances elsewhere
Thin wallsDeflect under the tool and clamp; distort after releaseIncrease wall thickness where possible; support thin sections during machining
Fine or load-bearing threadsSoft thread flanks deform and strip under load and creepPrefer coarse threads; use metal inserts or through-bolts for load-bearing joints
Long-term interference fitsPTFE creeps, so press-fit grip falls over timeAdd mechanical retention (shoulder, circlip, flange) rather than relying on interference alone
Sharp internal cornersStress concentration; hard to machine cleanlySpecify an internal radius
Unspecified measurement temperatureThe same part measures differently in a cool and a warm roomState the temperature at which dimensions apply

Threads

Threads can be cut in PTFE, but they are weak and creep under sustained load. Coarse threads are more robust than fine ones. For joints that must stay tight — or be assembled and disassembled repeatedly — use a metal insert, a through-bolt with a nut, or a design in which the PTFE is clamped rather than threaded.

Thin walls and press-fits

Thin-walled sleeves and bushes are among the hardest PTFE parts to make accurately, because they deflect during machining and distort when released. When a PTFE bush is pressed into a housing, its bore also closes in — allow for this by finish-machining the bore after fitting, or by sizing it with the expected closure in mind. Because PTFE creeps, add mechanical retention rather than relying on interference alone.

What to put on the drawing

  1. Material and grade — virgin PTFE, or the filler and percentage (see virgin vs filled PTFE).
  2. Dimensions and tolerances, with critical dimensions clearly identified.
  3. Reference temperature at which dimensions apply.
  4. Surface finish on sealing and running faces.
  5. Edge treatment — chamfers, radii and permissible burr.
  6. Stress relief requirement, if any.
  7. Service conditions — temperature, media and mating parts — so the machinist understands the function.
  8. Inspection requirements and quantity.

The more a supplier understands about how the part works, the better the advice they can give on tolerances, grade and stock form. A note on function is often more useful than an extra decimal place.
